guideTitle: Best Solar Generators with a 50 Amp Outlet (2026)
metaTitle: Solar Generators with a 50 Amp Outlet
metaDescription: Six solar generators with 120/240V output that can serve a 50 amp outlet, with honest notes on 14-50 receptacles, adapters and real continuous amps.
expertTake: The BLUETTI Apex 300 with the B300K battery is the best pick because it delivers simultaneous 120V and 240V and grows by stacking units instead of rewiring. The EcoVolt P5000 Plus is the value route to 240V with a 5,120Wh tank. Skip any 120V-only station if the outlet you need is a true 240V 50 amp receptacle, because the plug shape alone does not give you the voltage.
introParagraphs: A fifty amp outlet is built for two hot legs, which means it expects 240 volts, and most portable batteries only make 120. That mismatch is the reason this category is full of misleading listings, and it is the first thing to settle before comparing any specs.

We looked for solar generators that genuinely offer split-phase or paralleled 240V output, and we dropped generator cords, inlet boxes and gas inverter units that crowd the search results. The six that remain are ranked by how cleanly they deliver the voltage, the energy and the solar input a real outlet job needs.

products.name: BLUETTI Apex 300 with B300K Battery and Hub D1, 2,764.8Wh
products.description:
The Apex 300 is modular in a way the others are not. A single unit offers 120V and 240V output at the same time, so a 14-50 style outlet and ordinary 120V sockets can both be live, and the listing says two or three units can be paralleled to reach 5.5 to 8.3kWh. That makes it easy to start small and grow, without replacing the inverter.

The bundle here adds the B300K battery and a DC hub with a 50A Anderson port, two cigarette lighter ports, two DC5521 ports and USB-C and USB-A, which is a useful low-voltage center for an RV or a van. At 3,840W it holds more output per unit than the 3,600W boxes, though its single-unit tank is smaller than the P5000 Plus's 5,120Wh.

The tradeoff is complexity. A stacked system needs correct cabling and the right hub, and you should read the manual before the first outage. Keep the stack cool and dry, store the batteries around half charged and check each connector for tightness every season. Because the hub and battery arrive as separate pieces, lay out the cabling on a bench first and label every connector before you stack anything.
products.bestFor: Owners who want 240V now and the freedom to add batteries later.
pros: DC hub with a 50A Anderson port
cons: Costs rise quickly with each module

products.name: EcoVolt P5000 Plus 5,120Wh 120/240V Power Station
products.description:
The P5000 Plus pairs a big 5,120Wh tank with dual-voltage output, and it does so without the premium of the household brands. Five AC outlets, 3,600W of continuous power and a 5,000W surge cover most 240V jobs, though the 3,600W rating means a full 50 amp load is out of reach.

Charging is generous: an 1,800W AC input and up to 1,000W of solar mean a good day of sun nearly refills a quarter of the tank, and the listing says it uses automotive-grade LiFePO4. Against the Oscal PowerMax 6000 it holds 1,520Wh more energy but produces 2,400W less, a trade that favors long runs over big starts.

Brand history is thin, so treat the first weeks as a burn-in: run real loads, watch the fans and keep the receipt. Place it on a dry, solid surface, keep the vents clear and store it half charged. Its 1,000W solar input makes a ground-mount array of five to six panels worth considering if the unit lives at a cabin.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a big 240V-capable battery without the household-brand price.
cons: 3,600W continuous cannot fill a 50 amp outlet
Brand has a short track record

products.name: GROWATT HELIOS 3600 3,600Wh LFP, 240V/7,200W Parallel
products.description:
Growatt is a name from the solar-inverter industry, and the Helios reflects it. One unit delivers 3,600W; connect two in parallel and the listing says you get 240V at 7,200W, which can run heavy appliances like an air conditioner or a dryer. That is a cleaner route to a true 50 amp-class load than any single 120V box.

The sub-15ms EPS function switches critical loads to battery quickly, and the cold-start technology helps charging in low temperatures. The listing's claim of up to 15 hours of power for daily home devices is a reminder that this is a home backup design first.

Compared with the Apex 300 it needs two units for 240V, so cost doubles, but its capacity ceiling of 36kWh is far higher. Plan for a flat, ventilated spot for both units, label the cables and test the pair under load before the season. Treat the two units as a matched pair, and replace or service them together so their firmware and battery health stay aligned.
products.bestFor: Home and cabin owners who want to build a 240V system from two identical units.
cons: You must buy two units for 240V
Less accessory support than major brands

products.name: OSCAL PowerMax 6000 with 3x400W Panels, 6,000W 120/240V
products.description:
This is the highest-output single box here, with 6,000W at 120/240V and a 9,000W surge. At 240V that is 25 amps, half of what a 50 amp outlet can carry, but far more than any other unit can supply from one chassis. Four AC outlets and the split-phase inverter let a dryer, an air conditioner and a well pump run from one machine.

The listing quotes 2,400W of solar input and a full charge in about 1.44 hours using wall plus solar together, and three 400W panels come in the kit. The tank is the weak link at 3,600Wh, which empties in about an hour under a heavy load.

Set the panels up on the ground, where they can be tilted and cleaned, and confirm the unit sits in a dry, ventilated spot. Check the connectors seasonally. Against the P5000 Plus you get nearly double the output but 1,520Wh less energy. The four AC outlets are enough for a pump, a dryer and a few small loads, but spread them across both legs.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want high 240V output and a big solar array in one purchase.

products.name: ABOK Ark3600 3,840Wh with 400W Solar Panel
products.description:
Not every 50 amp outlet needs 240V. Some, like an EV charger or an RV on one leg, need only a heavy 120V feed, and for that the Ark3600 is a capable and economical choice. It delivers 3,600W continuously with 4,500W peak, and the 3,840Wh tank is larger than the Apex 300's.

The listing quotes 2,000W of solar input and a 400W panel in the box, and expansion to 11,520Wh. It makes no 240V claim, so this is a one-leg unit and you should not buy it for a dryer or a well pump.

Use it with a correctly rated 50 amp adapter, and do not pull more than 2,880W continuously through it. Check the vents and cables each season and keep the battery partly charged in storage. Because it is a single-leg design, balance matters little, which makes it simpler than a split-phase setup.
products.bestFor: Buyers who need a heavy 120V feed to a 50 amp outlet and want a big tank.
cons: Newer platform with fewer owner reports

products.name: PECRON F3000LFP 3,072Wh 3,600W Power Station
products.description:
The F3000LFP is here as the honest option for anyone whose 50 amp outlet only needs a strong 120V feed. It delivers 3,600W of pure sine output through six AC outlets, so several appliances plug in directly, and the listing says it powers 13 devices at once, including refrigerators and heavy-duty appliances.

Its best trait is recharge speed: zero to full in about two hours from an 1,800W wall input, which is quicker than the larger tanks in this guide. At 3,072Wh it holds 768Wh less than the ABOK Ark3600 and has no 240V claim, so it cannot run a dryer or a pump.

Use a properly rated adapter between its outlet and a 50 amp receptacle, and keep sustained loads under about 2,880W. Rest it at half charge, keep the intake clear and top it up every few months.
products.bestFor: People who want fast recharging and many outlets for a heavy single-leg load.
pros: Zero to full in about two hours
Six AC outlets plus USB-C and car ports
cons: Smaller tank than the ABOK Ark3600
Shorter support history than major brands

buyingCriteria.explanation: A 50 amp outlet can be a 120/240V receptacle or a single-leg connection. The Apex 300, P5000 Plus and Oscal PowerMax 6000 output 240V, the Helios 3600 does as a pair, while the Ark3600 and Pecron are 120V only. The plug fits either way, so check the voltage listing. A labelled breaker panel at the outlet tells you whether the circuit is truly 240V.

Amps equal watts divided by volts. The Oscal's 6,000W at 240V is 25 amps, a paired Helios 3600's 7,200W is 30 amps, and the P5000 Plus's 3,600W is 15 amps. A true 50 amp supply is 12,000W, so none of these fills the circuit.

Electrical codes treat continuous loads as 80 percent of the breaker, so a 50 amp circuit is planned for 40 amps. You are unlikely to approach that with a battery, but cables and adapters must still be rated for the amps you do draw.
A 240V dryer uses 3,000 to 5,000W and drains a 3,600Wh battery in under an hour. The P5000 Plus's 5,120Wh gives a meaningfully longer run, and stacking the Apex 300 to 8.3kWh adds more.

The Oscal accepts 2,400W of solar, the P5000 Plus 1,000W and the ABOK 2,000W. A bigger input only helps if you own the panels, so compare it with the array you plan to buy. Real output is 60 to 80 percent of nameplate.

Moving from a battery to a 14-50 receptacle usually means an adapter or a custom cord. Use 6 gauge or heavier cable for 50 amp runs and avoid thin adapters. A cheap, undersized cable is a heat hazard. Keep the cord short, since voltage drop on a long thin run wastes watts.

specDecoder.meaning: Two 120V legs forming 240V, as a 50 amp RV or range outlet expects.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Apex 300, P5000 Plus and Oscal 6000 offer it, and the Helios 3600 as a pair.

specDecoder.meaning: Divide continuous watts by voltage. It shows how much of a 50 amp circuit you actually use.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Oscal's 6,000W at 240V is 25A, the P5000 Plus's 3,600W is 15A.

specDecoder.meaning: Two units combined to produce higher voltage or wattage.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Helios 3600 gives 240V at 7,200W as a pair; the Apex 300 stacks two or three.

specDecoder.meaning: The most panel power the station accepts at once.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Oscal lists 2,400W and the P5000 Plus 1,000W.

specDecoder.meaning: Extra battery modules that add watt-hours.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Apex 300 stacks to 8.3kWh, the Helios 3600 to 36kWh.

howWeEvaluated.title: Voltage honesty
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked whether each unit truly lists 240V or paired 240V output. The Apex 300, P5000 Plus and Oscal passed, the Helios needs a pair, and the ABOK and Pecron failed.

howWeEvaluated.title: Share of a 50 amp circuit
howWeEvaluated.description: We converted rated watts to amps at 240V. A paired Helios 3600 fills about 60 percent of the circuit, the Oscal 50 percent and the P5000 Plus 30 percent.

howWeEvaluated.title: Energy and expansion
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared tank sizes and growth paths. The P5000 Plus tops the single-unit group, while the Apex 300 and Helios 3600 win on modularity.

howWeEvaluated.title: Solar compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered solar input limits and included panels. The Oscal and ABOK lead on input, the P5000 Plus on its 1,000W input.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We used listing details and owner feedback patterns for support and weight, not our own ownership. We also noted whether replacement battery modules are likely to stay available.

howToChoose.subheading: Single Box vs Two Paired Units

cards.label: Single box
cards.text: The Oscal and P5000 Plus give 240V from one chassis. It is simpler to set up and wire, but you cannot split the load between two places.

cards.label: Paired units
cards.text: The Helios 3600 pair and the stacked Apex 300 give modular 240V. You can start with one and scale, but each module adds cost and cabling.

howToChoose.note: Choose a single box for simplicity and a pair or stack if you plan to grow.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for 240V output and a tank above 5kWh. A level 2 EV charger on a 50 amp outlet draws about 7,000W at full speed, so you will need a charger set to a lower amp limit.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The P5000 Plus has the biggest tank here and 240V. A 15 amp charge adds roughly 12 miles of range per hour, so expect a slow top-up.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You need a true 240V supply for a dryer, a pump or an RV. The Oscal or a paired Helios 3600 gives the output.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You only need heavy 120V. The ABOK Ark3600 does it for less.

maintenance.why: A quick reading confirms 240V between the hot legs and 120V from each to neutral. Write the reading on a tag attached to the cord for future reference.
Heavy gauge cords carry the current safely, and scorched pins signal trouble.
LiFePO4 cells age slowest at moderate charge.
Large inverters move a lot of air, and dust shortens full-load runtime.
Stacked modules rely on tight connectors, and loose ones heat up.

faq.q: Does a 50 amp plug mean the solar generator can supply 50 amps?
faq.a: No. The plug describes the connector, not the battery. A paired Helios 3600 supplies about 30 amps at 240V, the Oscal 25 amps.

faq.q: Do I need 240V for a 50 amp outlet?
faq.a: For a dryer, range or a full RV, yes. A 120V station can feed one leg of an RV or a heavy 120V appliance, but it cannot run 240V loads. If you are unsure which your outlet is, read the label on the breaker and the receptacle before buying.

faq.q: Which is the best value with 240V?
faq.a: The EcoVolt P5000 Plus offers 240V and 5,120Wh at a lower cost than a paired Helios 3600. The Oscal adds output and panels. Neither is a casual purchase, so match the choice to how often you will actually use 240V.

faq.q: Can these charge an electric vehicle?
faq.a: Slowly. A 15 amp level 2 charge from the P5000 Plus delivers about 3,600W. It is a top-up solution, not a replacement for a wall charger. Check your car's onboard charger limit, which often caps lower than the outlet.

faq.q: Are generator cords and inlet boxes included?
faq.a: No. Those are accessories for gas generators and are not solar generators. Buy a cord rated for your outlet separately.

faq.q: How many batteries do I need to stack?
faq.a: Add up the daily watt-hours of your 240V loads. A 2,765Wh Apex 300 supports a few hours of a dryer, while three stacked units reach about 8.3kWh. Stacking also gives you redundancy, since a single module can still run alone if another needs service.
